content: Amblyomma maculatum, commonly referred to as the Gulf Coast tick, is a species of tick that is frequently associated with the transmission of Rickettsia spotted fevers. The life cycle of a tick consists of four distinct stages: the egg (hatching), the six-legged nymph, the eight-legged nymph, and the adult stage. Ticks require a blood meal at each stage of their life cycle to survive and progress to the next stage. Hosts for these blood meals can include mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians. Ticks often switch between different hosts during their life cycle. Humans are most commonly targeted during the nymph and adult stages. The life cycle of ticks is influenced by seasonal variations. For example, eggs hatch into larvae during the summer months, and these larvae typically infect birds or rodents. The larvae remain with their host until the following spring, at which point they molt into nymphs. During the nymph stage, ticks often seek mammalian hosts, including humans. Nymphs stay with their host until the fall, when they transition into adults. Adult ticks prefer larger mammals, such as deer or livestock, over smaller rodents. The average tick life cycle spans approximately three years, although variations exist depending on the species. Ticks require blood meals to progress through their life cycle. On average, a tick spends 10 minutes to 2 hours preparing to feed. During feeding, the tick injects anesthetic properties into its host via its saliva, making the bite painless. A feeding tube is inserted into the host, and an adhesive-like substance secures the tick to the host during the blood meal. Ticks feed for several days, ingesting the host's blood and potentially acquiring pathogens. After feeding, the tick detaches and seeks a new host, transferring any pathogens it carries during subsequent feedings. Amblyomma maculatum primarily infests small mammals and ground-dwelling birds during its immature stages. Cotton rats are particularly favored hosts. Documented hosts include species such as Geothlypis trichas, Cardinalis cardinalis, Passerina ciris, Sialia sialis, Thryothorus ludovicianus, Troglodytes aedon, Zonotrichia albicollis, domestic dogs (Canis lupus familiaris), fallow deer (Dama dama), humans (Homo sapiens), eastern woodrats (Neotoma floridana), white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus), marsh rice rats (Oryzomys palustris), cotton mice (Peromyscus gossypinus), hispid cotton rats (Sigmodon hispidus), pigs (Sus scrofa), and marsh rabbits (Sylvilagus palustris). In 2013, Rickettsia parkeri, the causative agent of American tick bite fever, was detected in a female Amblyomma maculatum collected at Bombay Hook National Wildlife Refuge in Delaware. This marked the first evidence of this pathogen's association with this tick species in the state. Geographically, Amblyomma maculatum is predominantly found in coastal areas of the United States, particularly along the Atlantic Coast and the Gulf of Mexico. Preventing tick exposure is challenging, as it is unrealistic to completely avoid activities in tick-prone areas. Therefore, personal protection measures are essential when in natural environments where ticks are present. These measures include wearing light-colored clothing to make ticks more visible, tucking pant legs into socks to prevent ticks from crawling up, and applying repellents to discourage tick attachment. Permethrin-based repellents can be sprayed on clothing and boots, providing protection for several days. DEET-based repellents can be applied to the skin but require reapplication every few hours. Caution should be exercised when using DEET on children, as excessive application has been linked to adverse reactions. After returning from tick-prone areas, conduct a thorough body check using a mirror to inspect all parts of the body. Parents should carefully check their children, especially in the hair. Ticks can also be brought into the home on clothing or pets, so both should be examined to exclude ticks. To remove a tick, use fine-tipped tweezers or a notched tick extractor, and protect your fingers with tissue, paper towels, or latex gloves. Avoid using bare hands. Grasp the tick as close to the skin as possible and pull upward with steady, even pressure. Do not twist or jerk the tick, as this may cause its mouthparts to break off and remain in the skin. If this occurs, remove the mouthparts with tweezers. Consult a healthcare provider if illness develops. After removing the tick, disinfect the bite site thoroughly and wash your hands with soap and water. Do not squeeze, crush, or puncture the tick's body, as its fluids may contain infectious organisms. If skin is accidentally exposed to tick fluids, disinfect the area with iodine scrub, rubbing alcohol, or water containing detergents. Save the tick for identification in case illness occurs, as this may assist your doctor in making an accurate diagnosis. Place the tick in a sealable plastic bag and store it in your freezer. Write the date of the bite on a piece of paper and include it in the bag.
